episodes.title: A Bank Built Its Own Coding Agent. It Took Off — Felipe Felisola Caso & Francesco Galletta, Monzo
episodes.description:
Monzo's in-house agent started as an emoji you could react with in Slack. Now it authors over 10% of all merged PRs across Monzo's tech teams and runs more than 1,800 tasks a day. Felipe and Francesco explain why it worked so fast. Their answer is the "lots of little multipliers" Monzo already had: an MCP gateway into internal tools and knowledge, a sandboxed agent orchestration system built for a regulated bank, and a platform that turns the agent itself into a building block. That building block now handles incidents, on-call data quality and requests from non-engineers.

episodes.title: Shipping AI Into 5 Major Banks Without a 12-Month Compliance Wait — Al Chen, Cisco
episodes.description:
Banks don't buy AI software until it survives their security and compliance review. Al Chen shares what it took to deploy inside five major banks without a year-long bottleneck. He covers the build pipeline, CVE remediation with agents writing and testing exploits, backup and restore verification, PII leaking through LLM judges, and why zero leakage and data sovereignty are never free.

episodes.title: Why AI Agents Will Need Their Own Bank Accounts — Lincoln Murr, Coinbase
episodes.description:
Lincoln Murr, head of AI product at Coinbase, explains agentic finance: agents that pay with money and agents that grow it. He covers the path from AgentKit, an early experiment giving an AI a wallet, to x402, an open standard built on the long-unused HTTP 402 "payment required" code. x402 now handles hundreds of millions of agent transactions a month. Other topics are microtransactions as a replacement for the ad economy, agents running trades on simple instructions, and what two years of building taught Coinbase. Trust is earned step by step, and the AI is the enabler, not the product. He ends with a look at agents that can pay for their own upkeep.

episodes.title: How to Know When an AI Agent Can Work Unsupervised — Evan Kormos, Coinbase
episodes.description:
Evan Kormos, a player-coach at Coinbase with 15 years in enterprise financial services, lays out a practical way to bring agents into policy-driven, regulated workflows. He models processes as DAGs and loops, explains why a loop is only as trustworthy as its check, and shows how evals and traces become a new confidence mechanism. Agents then move through three stages: fully supervised, then sampled, then humans handling only exceptions.

episodes.title: Smarter Models Killed the Harness. Here's What's Left — Jediah Katz, SpaceXAI
episodes.description:
Is the agent harness dead? Jediah Katz, Cursor's longest-tenured agent-harness engineer and now at SpaceX, explains why fancy harnesses no longer add coding intelligence: the data flywheel teaches models the skills harnesses used to patch in. He then argues why the harness matters more than ever. It opens new frontiers like Grokbot, and it owns what models can't absorb: infrastructure, trust and security, and efficiency. He closes with predictions, including that 90% of agent work runs off the laptop within six months.

episodes.title: The Model Swap Workshop: GPT-5.5 vs Kimi vs DeepSeek vs Mistral — Pamela Fox, Microsoft
episodes.description:
Benchmarks won't tell you how a model behaves in your app. Swapping it in and testing will.

NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT
Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes

Pamela Fox, Principal Cloud Advocate at Microsoft, runs the same scenarios against GPT-5.5, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash and Mistral Large 3 on Microsoft Foundry so you can see where models differ and what you can do about it. She works up from a letter-counting prompt to RAG groundedness, image input, multilingual pitfalls, tool calling, tool calling in a loop and a LangChain v1 travel agent, then moves to evaluation: string-check evals, LLM-as-a-judge, Microsoft's new ASSERT tool for generating test sets from a spec, and DSPy prompt optimization that finds a prompt the cheapest model can satisfy.

In this video:
- Where top models differ: counting, groundedness, vision, tool calls and parallel tool calling
- How prompt engineering closes some gaps but not image understanding
- Bulk evals with string checks and LLM-as-a-judge
- Generating test sets with ASSERT and optimizing prompts with DSPy

episodes.title: Version-Controlled Search: The Web as It Was — Ryan Ahern, Exa
episodes.description:
Ryan Ahern of Exa introduces Exa Snapshot, which lets agents search the web as it looked on any past date. He covers why search quality matters when agents broker most searches, how snapshot results compare to live results, and how teams use point-in-time search to build and test predictive signals without overfitting.

episodes.title: Backtest Your Agent Against Yesterday's Web — Ryan Ahern, Exa
episodes.description:
How do you know whether your agent would have made the right call? Ryan Ahern of Exa shows how to use version-controlled search to see the web exactly as it was on a past date, then backtest an agent's predictions against what actually happened. The hands-on example predicts company acquisitions from signals like leadership turnover, then tunes the system without leaking future information.
